description:
Found by cold review of fz-5xp.15.

    defmodule Integer do defstruct [:v] end
    fn main(), do: dbg(to_string(7))

    error[resolve/unknown-import]: module `Integer` does not export `to_string/1`
      --> runtime:StringChars.fz:29:24

The user's `defstruct` wins `classify_impl_target` (src/compiler2/world.rs),
so the RUNTIME LIBRARY's own `StringChars.Integer` impl body now resolves
`Integer.to_string(i)` against the user's module. The only span in the
diagnostic points at runtime-library source; the user's `defmodule` is never
mentioned. Same for `Float` and `Atom`. Elixir warns about redefining the
module and then works.

Softer sibling, no diagnostic at all: a user `defmodule Integer` WITHOUT a
defstruct silently REPLACES the runtime module -- `Integer.to_string/1`
disappears -- and if the user's module happens to define `to_string/1` it
silently becomes the `StringChars.Integer` impl.

PRE-EXISTING MECHANISM, newly reachable: before fz-5xp.15 no runtime module was
named after a builtin value family, so nothing depended on the collision. Now
`Atom`, `Integer` and `Float` all are.

DONE = a user module shadowing a runtime-library module is either diagnosed at
the user's own span or namespaced so it cannot capture the library's internal
calls. Not "the library should avoid those names": `Integer.to_string/1` is the
Elixir-parity spelling and the epic wants it.

Related: a user `defimpl` for a family the runtime library already implements is
silently IGNORED rather than overriding or erroring (verified with
`defimpl Enumerable, for: List`), which is the same question of who wins.
title: A user defstruct named Integer, Float or Atom silently captures the builtin family's protocol dispatch
